title: Disease-Specific Reporting: Why Nodal Nomenclature Matters
notes: Speaker notes and the full prose are in LECTURE.md. Slides keep only what is projected.
sharedStem: Does node A versus node B change management?
sharedOptions: Yes, changes how much the surgeon takes or how much the radiation field covers
Yes, takes surgery off the table or puts systemic therapy before surgery
Yes, changes intent from curative to palliative
lobbyNotes: Leave the QR up a full minute; residents arrive late. Say the session code out loud.
Everyone picks their year on the phone once. Then Begin.

pretest: **Order:** O to open the poll, let everyone vote, X to close, then Space to pick the hot seat (R3 or R4). They give their letter and one sentence of reasoning. Tap A–D to record it.
Say nothing beyond "noted" and move on. Your face does nothing during the pretest. No reveal; the answers appear only on the pre/post screen after the posttest.
quick: **Order:** Space to pick the hot seat first (R1), they answer aloud, then O to open the room vote, X to close, R to reveal. Anchoring is fine here; it is teaching, not measurement.
Quick checks test the rule on a case not shown in the pretest, never the pretest item itself.
posttest: Same question, same image, same options. No hot seat. O to open, close after about 45 seconds, → to move on. Do not reveal; after post4 press V for the pre/post screen.

items.title: For a PET/CT, first ask what disease is being staged.
body: - That decides which words matter.
- **Lymphoma:** nodal disease is defined by regions, the Ann Arbor classification.
- More specific language beyond the region is not needed.
- What counts is how many regions, and which side of the diaphragm.
- **Carcinomas:** nodal nomenclature is defined by a boundary.
- The boundary is different for different diseases.
- The nomenclature dictates the staging, which dictates the treatment.
> Lazy wording can unintentionally change the course of a patient's treatment.
notes: Build slide: each Next or right arrow reveals one line (8 presses), then moves on. Left arrow steps back a line.
Lymphoma reads nodes by region (Ann Arbor), so inside a region 'iliac' or 'axillary' is enough; what counts is how many regions and which side of the diaphragm.

Carcinomas read nodes against a boundary that differs by disease; the nomenclature sets the stage and the stage sets the treatment. Same scan: 'common iliac' for prostate, '4R' for lung, 'medial to pectoralis minor' for breast.
Land the last line: lazy wording quietly changes what the oncologist does.

items.title: Lymphoma counts regions
body: - One region is one area on this map. Nomenclature like “right iliac”, “mediastinal” and “right neck” is complete for staging purposes.
- Stage counts regions and sides of the diaphragm.
notes: Build: the map comes up alone. Press 1: the title. Press 2: one region is one area; the region name is the complete word. Press 3: stage counts regions and sides of the diaphragm. Point at the iliac and axillary regions while you say it.
Say it once: stage I one region, II two or more on one side of the diaphragm, III both sides, IV extranodal. Bulk and number of regions are what the lymphoma team wants from you.
Then the contrast: carcinomas do not use this map. They use a line, and the line is different for every disease. That is the next slide.

items.title: Three landmarks
body: - The common iliac bifurcation
- The left lateral wall of the trachea
- The pectoralis minor
Each one is a line where the same node changes its name and its consequence for the carcinoma. For lymphoma, none of them matter.
notes: These are the three lines you will learn to name today, one per case: prostate, lung, breast. Each is a boundary where the same node changes its name and its consequence, and for lymphoma none of them matter at all.
Say out loud: the pretest answers are coming, they were not expected to know them, and the point of the next 40 minutes is to make the posttest feel obvious.
Case 1 next.
items.caption: The three lines, one per case. Each comes back as its own slide.

items.title: The lazy sentence
body: > PSMA-avid right iliac lymph node, 1.2 cm.
Not wrong. Incomplete for this disease.
The urologist cannot tell whether this patient gets curative pelvic radiation or starts systemic therapy. They call you, or re-read the scan.
For lymphoma, the same sentence would have been complete.
notes: Put the lazy sentence up first. The urologist cannot tell from this whether the patient is a candidate for curative pelvic radiation or needs to start systemic therapy, so they call you or re-read the scan.
Say this out loud the first time: the sentence is not wrong, it is incomplete for this disease. For lymphoma the same sentence would have been complete.

items.title: The line: the common iliac bifurcation
items.caption: Coronal schematic. Gold line = the common iliac bifurcation, the edge of the pelvis for prostate cancer.
body: - Below the line (external, internal iliac, obturator): N1. Pelvic radiation with the prostate, curative intent.
- Above the line (common iliac, para-aortic): M1a. Systemic therapy leads.

- Aside: when M1a disease is limited to the common iliac nodes, there is evidence that radiation plus ADT may approach the outcomes of pelvic N1 disease treated the same way. The report still has to name the vessel so that conversation can happen.
- Lymphoma: one chain, one region. “Left iliac” and stop.
- Report the vessel the node sits on and which side of the bifurcation.
notes: Teach the line before the image. Walk the vessel tree top down: aorta, aortic bifurcation at L4, common iliac, then the bifurcation into external and internal iliac. The gold line is the common iliac bifurcation.

For prostate: below is N1 and radiated with the prostate; above is M1a and systemic therapy leads. Then the two contrasts on the right: bladder cancer keeps the common iliac node regional, lymphoma does not care.
An R1 who has this slide can answer the quick check (bladder, same node): the line does not matter for bladder.

Aside, said once: for M1a limited to the common iliac nodes, radiation plus ADT may do about as well as for pelvic N1; the field is extended rather than abandoned. Verify the trial you want to cite before naming it.

items.title: External iliac vs common iliac
items.caption: Fresh FDG PET/CT, read it as PSMA. Left: the vessels with bone removed. A sits on the external iliac just past the iliac bifurcation. B sits on the common iliac just past the aortic bifurcation.
body: # Lymphoma (DLBCL)
One iliac chain is one region. Above or below the bifurcation changes nothing. "Right iliac" and stop.
# Prostate
The bifurcation is the edge of the pelvis.
- Below it: radiated with the prostate, curative intent.
- Above it: counted as metastatic. Hormones and drugs instead.
The report must say which side of the bifurcation, with the vessel named.
notes: Fresh study, FDG standing in for PSMA. The left panel is the aorto-iliac tree with bone removed, with a line at each node's level; the axial CT and fused pairs are at those levels. B is the large node anterior-left of L5, just below where the aorta splits: a common iliac node. A is the node lateral to the left common iliac just below where it splits into external and internal: an external iliac node. Draw the bifurcation on the image (Z to zoom).
**Lymphoma:** the iliac chain on one side is one region. Above or below the bifurcation changes nothing; the report can say "right iliac" and stop.

**Prostate:** the bifurcation is the edge of the pelvis. Below it, the node gets radiated with the prostate. Above it, the node counts as metastatic and the patient goes to hormone therapy and drugs instead. The report has to say which side of the bifurcation, with the vessel named.
items.source: AutoPET PETCT_791ec15924, 2001-04-16, Melanoma. CT series 5.000000-GK p.v.2-41675, PET series 6.000000-PET corr.-15444. A: lesion #3 (10.6 mL, SUVmax 12.0, z 663 mm); B: lesion #4 (9.3 mL, SUVmax 13.8, z 702 mm).

items.title: Same node, different page
items.caption: NCCN Prostate Cancer v1.2027, PROS-7 and PROS-14
body: - Below the bifurcation: **N1**, the regional page. RT + ADT + abiraterone, curative intent.
- Above it: **M1a**, the metastatic page. Systemic therapy. RT to the primary only for low-volume disease.
notes: Prostate guideline, N1 on the regional page (PROS-7) and M1 on the metastatic page (PROS-14). "Same node, different page."

Verified against v1.2027: RT to the primary is still offered for synchronous low-volume mCSPC, and the low-burden definition explicitly includes nonregional node-only disease, so an M1a patient qualifies.

items.stem: New prostate cancer. PSMA-avid node along the right external iliac vessels, below the common iliac bifurcation. What goes in the report, and what happens to the patient?
options: Right external iliac node; regional, radiated with the prostate
Right common iliac node; metastatic, systemic therapy
Right pelvic node; management unchanged either way
Right iliac node; cannot say without the size
items.explain: Below the common iliac bifurcation the node is pelvic: name the vessel, external iliac, and it stays in the curative radiation plan. Above the bifurcation it would be a common iliac node and counted as metastatic.
items.imageCaption: The line: the common iliac bifurcation.

items.title: The lazy sentence
body: > FDG-avid paratracheal lymph node, 1.5 cm.
The thoracic surgeon cannot tell whether this patient is still theirs.
Right or left is the whole referral. The report did not say.
notes: The thoracic surgeon cannot tell whether this patient is still theirs. Right or left is the whole referral, and the report did not say.

items.title: The line: the left lateral wall of the trachea
items.caption: Axial schematic at the lower paratracheal level. Gold line = left tracheal wall, not the midline.
body: - Right and left paratracheal stations, 2R/2L and 4R/4L, are split by the left lateral wall of the trachea, not the midline.
- A node left of midline but medial to that wall is still 4R (or 2R).
- Same side as the tumor: N2, surgery may still be possible. Opposite side: N3, surgery off.
- Midline stations have no side: station 7 (subcarinal) is N2 for every tumor.
- Supraclavicular is N3 regardless of side.
- Lymphoma: the whole mediastinum is one region; sidedness means nothing.
notes: Teach the station rule before the image. The IASLC boundary between R and L paratracheal stations is the left lateral wall of the trachea, so a node sitting just left of midline is still right-sided.
Then the consequence: same side N2, opposite side N3. Name the exception, station 7 (subcarinal) is midline and always N2; that is the quick check.
If asked about 2 versus 4: the top of the aortic arch on the left, the innominate vein crossing on the right.

items.title: 4R vs 4L
items.caption: Fresh FDG PET/CT chest at the thoracic inlet. The teal line is the left lateral wall of the trachea. Not the midline.
body: # Lymphoma
The whole mediastinum is one region. Right or left changes nothing. The lymphoma team wants the size of the mass.
# Lung
- Same side as the tumor (N2): the surgeon is still in the room. Surgery may follow chemo-immunotherapy.
- Opposite side (N3): surgery is off the table. Chemoradiation.
A node left of midline but medial to the left tracheal wall is still 4R.
notes: Fresh FDG PET/CT chest. The teal line is drawn on the left lateral wall of the trachea, on both the CT and the fused panel. Not the midline: the left wall. The node anterior-right of the trachea is 2R; the node lateral to the line is 2L.
**Lymphoma:** the whole mediastinum is one region. Right or left paratracheal changes nothing; what the lymphoma team wants from the chest is how big the mass is.

**Lung:** the side of the node relative to the tumor is the decision. Same side, the surgeon is still in the room and the patient may still get an operation after chemo-immunotherapy. Opposite side, surgery is off the table and the patient gets chemoradiation.
A node just left of midline but medial to the left tracheal wall is still 4R, still same-side for a right lung tumor, so the report has to name the station, not describe the position.
items.source: AutoPET PETCT_db3daf78d2, 2000-10-30, Lymphoma. CT series 5.000000-GK p.v.2-47450, PET series 10.000000-PET corr.-51485. A: lesion #5 (7.1 mL, SUVmax 10.1, z -459 mm); B: lesion #9 (1.3 mL, SUVmax 8.0, z -453 mm).

items.title: Same side can still reach surgery. Opposite side cannot.
items.caption: NCCN Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer v9.2026
body: - **N2** (NSCL-10): chemoradiation, or systemic therapy then surgery if no progression. Fit, single-station, non-bulky N2 only.
- **N3** (NSCL-13): definitive concurrent chemoradiation.
notes: NSCLC stage III: the same-side branch (NSCL-10) that still reaches surgery and the opposite-side branch (NSCL-13) that goes to chemoradiation.
Footnote on NSCL-10: only selected N2 (fit, single-station, non-bulky, lobectomy only) goes systemic therapy then surgery. UCSF-specific practice not verified; say "may" not "will".

items.stem: Right upper lobe lung cancer. FDG-avid node just left of midline, but medial to the left lateral wall of the trachea. Station, and what does it mean?
options: 4L; opposite side, surgery off the table
Depends on the size of the node
items.explain: The border is the left lateral tracheal wall, not the midline. Medial to that wall is still 4R, same side for a right lung tumor, so the surgeon is still in the room.
items.imageCaption: The line: the left lateral wall of the trachea.

items.eyebrow: Case 2 · Aside, cut first if behind
items.title: One node, three services
body: The same superior mediastinal node is central-compartment disease for thyroid cancer and goes to the thyroid surgeon.
- Lung: station and side rule
- Lymphoma: one region, report the size
- Thyroid: central compartment, neck dissection
notes: Cut this first if behind. The same superior mediastinal node is central-compartment disease for thyroid cancer and goes to the thyroid surgeon. One node, three services.

items.title: The lazy sentence
body: > FDG-avid left axillary lymph node, 1.4 cm.
The breast surgeon books a sentinel node procedure.
If that node was medial to the pectoralis minor, the patient should have gone to medical oncology first. The report is the reason they did not.
notes: The breast surgeon books a sentinel node procedure. If that node was medial to the pectoralis minor, the patient should have gone to medical oncology first, and the report is the reason they did not.

items.title: The line: the pectoralis minor
items.caption: Axial schematic of the left axilla. Gold = pectoralis minor; levels are named by their relation to it.
body: - Level I lateral, level II behind, level III medial to pectoralis minor. Rotter’s sits between the two pectoralis muscles.
- Breast: level I or II is the surgeon’s axilla. Level III (infraclavicular): cN3a, systemic therapy before any surgery. Rotter’s is not reached by a standard dissection, so it changes the operation.
- Lymphoma: axillary and pectoral (including Rotter’s) are one region; infraclavicular is a separate region.
- Lymphoma: infraclavicular alone or axillary alone is one region, same stage. Both together is two regions and the stage goes up.
notes: Teach the muscle before the image. On an axial, find the pectoralis minor as the oblique band from the coracoid to ribs 3 to 5; everything lateral is level I, deep is level II, medial is level III.

Consequence for breast cancer: I and II go to the surgeon, III sends the patient to medical oncology first. Rotter's and internal mammary have to be named because the standard operation does not reach them.
The quick check (node deep to pectoralis minor) is level II, surgeon first, straight from this slide.

items.title: Two lines on the pectoralis minor
items.caption: Normal CT at the glenoid. Gold: the medial and lateral borders of the pectoralis minor.
body: - **Level I**: lateral to the pectoralis minor
- **Level II**: behind it, between the two lines
- **Level III**: medial to it, under the clavicle
- **Rotter’s**: between pectoralis major and minor. A different name, and a different problem.
notes: Build: the CT with the two lines comes up alone. Press 1: a node lateral to the lateral line is level I. Press 2: a node behind the muscle, between the lines, is level II. Press 3: medial to the medial line is level III. Press 4: a node between pectoralis major and minor is Rotter’s.
The circles mark positions, not real nodes; this is a normal axilla.

items.title: Rotter's vs level II
body: # Lymphoma
Same region, same stage, same treatment. "Axillary" and stop.
# Breast
Same stage. Not the same operation.
A standard axillary dissection does not reach the interpectoral space. An unreported Rotter's node is a node left behind, and radiation has to cover it separately.
> The stage did not change. The surgeon's plan did.
notes: **Lymphoma:** same region, same stage, same treatment. The report can say "axillary" and stop.

**Breast:** same stage too, but not the same operation. A standard axillary dissection does not reach the interpectoral space, so an unreported Rotter's node is a node left behind, and radiation planning covers it separately. The stage did not change; the surgeon's plan did.
(The 8% interpectoral metastasis figure is from a 1984 series; label it as such or leave the number out.)

items.title: Level II vs level III
body: # Lymphoma
Different regions, but one region is one region. A single node at II or at III is the same stage and the same treatment.
# Breast
II versus III is the whole decision.
- Level II: the surgeon.
- Medial to pectoralis minor: the medical oncologist first. Chemotherapy before any operation, and the radiation plan expands.
Say which side of the muscle before the case is booked.
notes: **Lymphoma:** different regions, but one region is one region. A single node at level II or at level III is the same stage and the same treatment, so II versus III does not change the plan.

**Breast:** II versus III is the whole decision. Level II goes to the surgeon. A node medial to the pectoralis minor sends the patient to the medical oncologist first, for chemotherapy before any operation, and the radiation plan expands. The report has to say which side of the muscle before the case is booked.

items.title: Versus is not plus: II and III together
body: Now both diseases care, for different reasons.
- **Lymphoma**: two regions instead of one. The stage goes up.
- **Breast**: level III is involved, so it is the chemo-first pathway. Level II riding along adds nothing.
Versus and plus are different questions, and the two diseases answer them in opposite order.
notes: Now both diseases care, for different reasons. Lymphoma: two regions instead of one, so the stage goes up. Breast: level III is involved, so it is the chemo-first pathway, and level II riding along adds nothing.
Versus and plus are different questions, and the two diseases answer them in opposite order.

items.title: cN3 goes to systemic therapy first
items.caption: NCCN Invasive Breast Cancer v9.2026, BINV-L and ST-2
body: - Inoperable upfront: inflammatory, bulky or matted cN2, **cN3**, cT4. Preoperative systemic therapy.
- cN3a is the infraclavicular, level III, node.
- Operable ER-positive HER2-negative disease at cN1 goes to the surgeon first. HER2-positive and triple-negative at cN1 do not.
notes: Breast: the candidates for preoperative systemic therapy page (BINV-L). Inoperable upfront includes cN3; cN3a is the infraclavicular, level III, node (ST-2).

Be precise if asked: for operable disease, preop therapy is *preferred* for HER2-positive and triple-negative at cN1 or larger. The "level II goes to surgery first" claim holds because the case is ER-positive HER2-negative.

items.stem: Left breast cancer. FDG-avid node medial to the pectoralis minor, under the clavicle. Level, and who sees the patient first?
options: Level III; medical oncology first, systemic therapy before surgery
Level I; surgeon first, sentinel node
items.explain: Medial to the pectoralis minor is level III, infraclavicular: cN3a. That puts systemic therapy before any surgery. Lateral to the muscle is level I, behind it level II, the surgeon's axilla.

items.title: Even lymphoma has more than one map
body: The Hodgkin trial groups count nodal areas differently from the standard regions. The same axilla can be one area on one scheme and two on another.
The counting rule belongs to the trial, not to anatomy.
notes: Cut if behind. Even lymphoma has more than one map. The Hodgkin trial groups count nodal areas differently from the standard regions, so the same axilla can be one area on one scheme and two on another. The counting rule belongs to the trial, not to anatomy.

items.title: Three reporting rules
body: - **Use the disease's own vocabulary.** Station for lung, level for breast and neck, region for lymphoma, named vessel for the pelvis.
- **Give the short-axis size.**
- **Say which side of the boundary the node is on, and name the boundary.**
If the history does not tell you the primary, say which classification you used. The same sentence will be read by three services.
notes: Use the disease's own vocabulary: station for lung, level for breast and neck, region for lymphoma, named vessel for the pelvis. Give the short-axis size. Say explicitly which side of the boundary the node is on, and name the boundary.
If the clinical history does not tell you the primary, say which classification you used, because the same sentence will be read by three different services.
Posttest next: same three questions, same images, same order. No hot seat. Open each poll, close after about 45 seconds, move on without revealing. Then V for the pre/post reveal.
